meta.title: Overfitting and Bias-Variance
meta.thesis: Overfitting and Bias-Variance is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A churn model looks excellent on training data but fails after a marketing campaign changes user behavior. By the end, they should be able to build or review bias-variance diagnosis worksheet with train/validation gaps, measure generalization gap on recent holdout data, and catch the failure where the model memorizes quirks instead of learning durable signal.

mentalMap.title: Overfitting and Bias-Variance: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Diagnose model generalization using training error, validation error, bias, variance, regularization, and final test discipline.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Overfitting and bias-variance are ways to explain why a model can fit data yet fail new cases.

modules.title: Generalization is the real target
modules.sub: A model is useful when it performs on examples it did not fit.
modules.summary: Overfitting is a failure of generalization, not a failure to memorize.
objectives: Explain why low training error can be misleading.
Anchor the lesson in a churn prediction case.

blocks.title: The exam is future data

spans.text: Problem anchor: a subscription team trains a churn model. A very flexible model gets 99 percent accuracy on historical customers, but fails on the next month. It learned quirks of the old data instead of patterns that generalize.

Generalization means performance on examples not used for fitting. Overfitting happens when the model adapts too closely to training noise, leakage, or accidental patterns. Underfitting happens when the model is too simple to capture important structure.

blocks.analogy: Training data is homework; validation and test data are exams with new questions.

blocks.title: Case study: churn model memorizes promo codes

spans.text: The model learns that customers with a one-time promo code from a past campaign churned less. In the future campaign, the code changes. Training performance looked excellent because the old code was a shortcut. Validation on a later month reveals the shortcut does not transfer.

blocks.title: Generalization
blocks.prompt: Why can very low training error be bad news?

options.text: It proves the model is unbiased and fair.
It may mean the model memorized noise or leakage that will not appear in new data.
It means validation is unnecessary.

blocks.explanation: Training error alone cannot answer the future-data question.

modules.title: Bias and variance describe two failure shapes
modules.sub: One model is too rigid; another is too sensitive.
modules.summary: Bias-variance language links error patterns to model capacity.
objectives: Distinguish high bias from high variance.
Map train/validation errors to each failure.
Choose the first fix for each pattern.

blocks.title: High bias misses the pattern; high variance chases noise

spans.text: High bias means the model is too constrained for the true pattern: both training and validation errors are high. High variance means the model fits training data very well but changes too much with the sample: training error is low and validation error is high.

options.name: High train and validation error

cells.text: richer features, more flexible model, better objective

options.whenToUse: The model misses even training examples.

options.name: Low train, high validation error

cells.text: regularization, more data, simpler model, leakage audit

options.whenToUse: Training looks great but validation fails.

cells.text: evaluate final test and monitor drift

modules.title: Validation curves expose memorization
modules.sub: Curves show what happens as model capacity changes.
modules.summary: Comparing train and validation curves makes overfitting visible.
objectives: Explain validation curves in plain language.
Spot the capacity where validation stops improving.
Avoid tuning on the test set.

blocks.title: Capacity is a dial, not a trophy

spans.text: As model capacity increases, training error often falls. Validation error may fall at first, then rise when the model begins to fit noise. The best capacity is usually near the validation minimum, not the lowest training error.
Depth 2 tree: train error 0.22, validation error 0.24. Depth 6: train 0.10, validation 0.15. Depth 20: train 0.01, validation 0.23. Depth 6 is the candidate; depth 20 memorizes historical quirks.

blocks.title: Curve choice
blocks.prompt: Which tree depth should you choose from the worked curve?

options.text: Depth 20, because training error is lowest.
Depth 6, because validation error is lowest even though training error is not.
Depth 2, because it is always safest.

modules.title: Regularization and data controls trade flexibility
modules.sub: The fix should match the failure mode, not the mood.
modules.summary: Regularization, simpler models, more data, and leakage audits address variance differently.
objectives: Choose regularization or data changes for overfitting.

blocks.title: Tiny capacity comparison for overfitting diagnosis
blocks.code:
results = [
    {"model": "linear", "train_error": 0.28, "val_error": 0.30},
    {"model": "tree_depth_6", "train_error": 0.10, "val_error": 0.15},
    {"model": "tree_depth_20", "train_error": 0.01, "val_error": 0.23},
]

best = min(results, key=lambda r: r["val_error"])
for r in results:
    gap = r["val_error"] - r["train_error"]
    diagnosis = "high variance" if gap > 0.12 else "reasonable gap"
    print(r["model"], "gap=", round(gap, 2), diagnosis)

print("choose", best["model"])

spans.text: This tiny report encodes the habit: compare train and validation, inspect the gap, and choose by validation rather than training error.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict which model is chosen and which model is flagged high variance.
predictThenReveal.answer: tree_depth_6 is chosen because it has the lowest validation error. tree_depth_20 is flagged high variance because its validation-training gap is large.

spans.text: Checklist: advice compares training and validation, checks leakage, names the likely failure mode, proposes a matching fix, and does not recommend using the test set for model selection.

modules.title: Test once, monitor drift later
modules.sub: The final estimate is not a tuning playground.
modules.summary: The test set gives a final pre-release estimate; production monitoring catches later change.
objectives: Explain why the test set stays untouched until the end.
Connect overfitting to drift and slice monitoring.
Define a release checklist for generalization.

blocks.title: You can overfit the test set too

spans.text: If the team repeatedly checks test performance while choosing features, thresholds, and model capacity, the test set becomes another validation set. The final estimate is no longer honest. After release, production data can drift, so monitoring and periodic re-evaluation are still needed.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Use validation to choose; use test to estimate; use monitoring to stay honest after release.
blocks.useWhen: Use this discipline when model choices, features, or thresholds are being compared.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid repeated test peeking, leakage-prone features, and aggregate-only metrics that hide failing slices.

blocks.title: Test discipline
blocks.prompt: Why not tune model capacity on the test set?

options.text: Because the test set should be used for gradient updates.
Because repeated test peeking makes the test estimate optimistic and less honest.
Because validation data is never useful.

blocks.explanation: The test set is reserved for the final generalization estimate.

ai.label: AI
ai.laymanDefinition: Software systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence.
ai.technicalNote: In these foundations lessons, AI is the broad field; the concrete mechanisms are models, data, objectives, and evaluation loops.

ml.label: ML
ml.laymanDefinition: A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of only following hand-written rules.
ml.technicalNote: ML work is defined by training data, features, models, objectives, validation, and deployment constraints.

model.label: Model
model.laymanDefinition: A learned or configured function that maps inputs to predictions, scores, clusters, or generated outputs.
model.technicalNote: Model choice encodes assumptions such as linearity, distance, tree splits, capacity, or sequential reward.

loss.label: Loss
loss.laymanDefinition: A numerical training signal that measures how wrong a prediction is for a task.
loss.technicalNote: Loss drives optimization; it is not the same as product quality, fairness, or final generalization.

generalization.label: Generalization
generalization.laymanDefinition: The ability of a model to perform well on examples it did not train on.
generalization.technicalNote: Generalization is checked with validation/test data, leakage audits, and slice monitoring.

pipeline.label: Pipeline
pipeline.laymanDefinition: A repeatable sequence of data transforms, feature steps, model fitting, and evaluation or inference.
pipeline.technicalNote: Pipelines prevent train/test leakage and keep preprocessing identical between training and production.

capstone.prompt: Take a small churn dataset and compare three model capacities. Plot or tabulate training and validation error, diagnose high bias or high variance, choose a regularization/data fix, and reserve the test set for one final estimate. Next rung: add cross-validation and slice metrics.
checks: Diagnosis uses both train and validation error.
Leakage is checked before celebrating high scores.
Regularization or data fixes match the failure mode.
Test data is not used for model selection.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: In your own words: a churn model scores 98% accuracy on training data but only 71% on new customers. What does this gap tell you, and what is the underlying problem called?
questions.acceptableAnswer: The gap indicates the model memorized the training data instead of learning general patterns — this is called overfitting (or poor generalization). High training accuracy with much lower validation/real-world accuracy is the classic overfitting signal.
questions.explanation: A large train-to-real-world accuracy gap is the defining symptom of overfitting: the model learned noise specific to training examples rather than patterns that transfer to unseen data.

questions.prompt: A churn model has HIGH training error AND high validation error. Which failure shape does this match, and what should you try first?

options.text: High variance — add more regularization or get more training data.
High bias — use a more complex model or add informative features.
High bias — reduce the training set so the model focuses on fewer examples.
High variance — remove regularization so the model can fit the data better.

questions.explanation: When both training and validation errors are high, the model is underfitting (high bias) — it lacks the capacity to capture the signal, so the first fix is to increase model complexity or enrich features, not to regularize further.

questions.prompt: On a validation curve, as model capacity increases, validation error first drops and then rises while training error keeps falling. What does the rising validation error tell you, and what capacity should you choose?

options.text: The model is underfitting at high capacity; choose the highest capacity tested.
The model is starting to memorize training noise; choose the capacity at the validation error minimum.
Validation error always rises with capacity, so the curve is uninformative.
The model needs more training data before the validation curve is meaningful.

questions.explanation: The point where validation error is lowest marks the sweet spot between underfitting and overfitting — beyond it, added capacity only helps the model memorize training examples, hurting generalization.

questions.prompt: Your overfitting simulation shows the decision tree memorizes training data perfectly. Which TWO actions are appropriate first responses? (Pick the single best answer that lists both.)

options.text: Evaluate on the held-out test set immediately, then tune based on those results.
Add L2 regularization (or limit tree depth) AND collect more labeled training examples.
Remove the validation set and retrain on all available data to reduce variance.
Switch to a simpler loss function and increase the learning rate.

questions.explanation: Regularization constrains model flexibility to reduce memorization, and more training data gives the model more genuine signal to learn from — both directly address overfitting without touching the test set.

questions.prompt: After deploying the churn model, the team notices it performs well on average but poorly on a specific customer segment (e.g., enterprise accounts). Which release-checklist practice would have caught this before deployment?

options.text: Running the test set evaluation multiple times and averaging the scores.
Slice monitoring — checking performance broken down by key subgroups on the held-out test set.
Tuning hyperparameters on the test set until the segment score improves.
Replacing the validation set with the enterprise-account subset and retraining.

questions.explanation: Slice monitoring evaluates model performance on meaningful subgroups (e.g., by segment, region, or plan type) before release, surfacing hidden failures that aggregate accuracy masks — a core item on a generalization release checklist.
